messages.content: I want to go to whistler for skiing. Can you give me the 5 day forecast for both the top and bottom of the mountain.

function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve data. This function is commonly used for API calls and web scraping. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The Date Nager API provides access holiday information for over 100 countries, including the ability to query for long weekends. It leverages ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country codes to tailor the search to your specific region of interest. More information can be found in https://date.nager.at/Api

headers.description: Optional headers to send with the request as a dictionary of header values.

Content-Type.description: The media type of the resource being requested, typically 'application/json'.

Authorization.description: The credentials to authenticate a user agent with a server, typically formatted as 'Bearer {token}'.

timeout.description: The maximum amount of time to wait for a response from the server, in seconds. A longer timeout may be necessary for slower network connections or overloaded servers. This is a float type value.

params.description: URL parameters to append to the URL. Sent as a dictionary of key-value pairs.

query.description: The query parameter for search or filtering.

page.description: The page number parameter for pagination. Used to retrieve a specific page of results.

auth.description: HTTP authentication credentials formatted as a (username, password) tuple.

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem), if required for the request.

cookies.description: Cookies to send with the request as a dictionary of cookie names and values.

sessionid.description: Session identifier cookie, used to recognize client sessions on the server.

csrftoken.description: CSRF protection token cookie, used to prevent cross-site request forgery attacks.

proxies.description: Proxy settings as a dictionary, mapping protocol or protocol and hostname to the URL of the proxy.

http.description: Proxy URL to use for HTTP requests, including the port number.

https.description: Proxy URL to use for HTTPS requests, including the port number.

stream.description: Whether to stream the download of the response. If False, the response content will be immediately downloaded. Streaming is useful for handling large files or responses.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate or not. Set to False to skip certificate verification, which is not recommended unless you are sure of the server's identity.

The user wants a 5-day forecast for both the top and bottom of Whistler Mountain. We need to provide weather forecast. We have no direct tool for weather. But we can use the requests_get function to call an API. There's no mention of a weather API. We could use open-meteo.com or weatherapi.com. But we don't have an API key. We might use open-meteo free API. Let's try open-meteo. For location, we need coordinates for Whistler. Whistler, BC, Canada. Coordinates approx 50.1167°N, 122.9578°W. We'll call open-meteo API: https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=50.1167&longitude=-122.9578&hourly=temperature_2m,precipitation,windspeed_10m&daily=weathercode,temperature_2m_max,temperature_2m_min,precipitation_sum&timezone=America/Vancouver&forecast_days=5. That returns daily forecast. But we need top and bottom of mountain. We might approximate top at higher elevation. But we can't get separate forecasts. We could approximate top at 2000m vs bottom at 500m. But open-meteo doesn't support altitude. We could use different lat/lon slightly offset? Not accurate.

We could use a weather API that supports altitude. Maybe WeatherAPI.com has a "history" but not altitude. Another approach: Use the "open-meteo" with "elevation" param? I think open-meteo has "elevation" param for some models. Actually open-meteo has "elevation" for "terrain" but not sure.

Alternatively, we can use the "weatherapi.com" free plan. But we don't have an API key. We could use "wttr.in" service via GET. For example: https://wttr.in/Whistler?format=j1. That returns JSON. Let's try that. We'll call requests_get with url "https://wttr.in/Whistler?format=j1". That returns JSON with "weather" array containing daily forecasts. That includes "maxtempC", "mintempC", "hourly" etc. But again no altitude.

We could approximate top and bottom by using "top" as "Whistler Blackcomb" and "bottom" as "Whistler Village". But we can't differentiate.

Maybe we can use "open-meteo" with "model=high_resolution" and "elevation" param. Actually open-meteo has "elevation" param for "terrain" but not sure.

Given constraints, we can provide a single forecast and note that top and bottom differences are minimal. Or we can provide two sets: one for "Whistler Village" and one for "Whistler Blackcomb" using different lat/lon. Let's approximate: Whistler Village lat 50.1167, lon -122.9578. Whistler Blackcomb lat 50.1167, lon -122.9578 too? Actually same. But maybe we can use "Whistler Blackcomb" as "Whistler Blackcomb" location. Let's try "https://wttr.in/Whistler%20Blackcomb?format=j1". That might return similar.

We'll call requests_get twice: once for "Whistler Village" and once for "Whistler Blackcomb". Then parse the JSON and extract daily forecast for next 5 days. Provide temperature ranges, precipitation probability, wind speed. Provide summary.

Let's do that.
